analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal excise tax on corporate stock buybacks from 1% to 4%.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have quadrupled the tax on corporate stock buybacks, was introduced in February 2023 with 10 Senate sponsors and died in the Finance Committee without ever receiving a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Corporations return cash to their shareholders by buying back their own stock, which pushes share prices up and mostly benefits large and wealthy holders. In 2022, Congress created a 1% tax on these repurchases. This bill would have quadrupled it to 4%, making buybacks more expensive for corporations and directing the revenue to the Treasury. It never moved after being sent to the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: The general public, in the form of added federal revenue from corporations and their largest shareholders; the tax falls on repurchases of stock, a form of shareholder payout that disproportionately benefits wealthy households and executive pay.

how_it_helps.text: The bill raises the rate of the excise tax on repurchases of corporate stock from 1 percent to 4 percent, raising more federal revenue from companies that buy back their own shares.
The tax applies to repurchases made after enactment, and the bill also adjusts how the tax base is calculated while exempting stock issued to certain covered employees from the adjustment rules.

analysis.who_pays: Publicly traded corporations that repurchase their own stock and, through lower after-tax proceeds, their shareholders — a group that skews wealthy, including executive and institutional investors.
analysis.who_pays_short: Corporations buying back stock and their shareholders

drawbacks.text: The tax is a blunt tool: it raises the cost of all stock repurchases, including those a company makes for ordinary corporate purposes such as offsetting employee stock plans, rather than distinguishing between buybacks that return cash and those that serve other functions.

An excise tax on buybacks can modestly raise companies' cost of returning cash, and some of the cost may reach ordinary investors through the mutual funds and retirement accounts that hold corporate stock.

The bill only changes a tax rate; it does not directly constrain executive compensation practices or direct the revenue to any specific public purpose, so its practical effect on working people is indirect and hard to measure.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — added federal revenue from a payout method used disproportionately by large corporations and wealthy shareholders — is real but modest in scale, and the 4% rate is low enough that it likely nudges corporate behavior rather than changing it sharply. The main cost falls on shareholders, including pension funds holding the same stocks, which spreads some of the burden more broadly than the bill's framing suggests. On balance it is a targeted tax increase on concentrated shareholders, not a sweeping reform.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Sherrod Brown introduced the bill on February 14, 2023, with six original cosponsors: Sens. Wyden, Schatz, Van Hollen, Reed, Lujan, and Baldwin.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day, which was its last action.
The Finance Committee never reported the bill out, and no vote on it occurred in either chamber before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
By the end of the Congress, the bill had 9 cosponsors, all Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations that repurchase large amounts of their own stock and their largest shareholders are better off, because the buyback tax stayed at 1% instead of rising to 4%.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies doing buybacks and major shareholders

for.name: Sens. Ron Wyden, Brian Schatz, Chris Van Hollen, Jack Reed, Ben Ray Lujan, and Tammy Baldwin
for.role: Original cosponsors; Wyden chaired the Senate Finance Committee to which the bill was referred
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction; no sponsor brought the bill to a vote in committee.

for.name: Three additional Democratic cosponsors
for.role: 9 total cosponsors by the end of the Congress, all Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: The committee of referral, chaired by a cosponsor of the bill
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill — no markup, no report — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.role: Majority-party leadership after January 2025; minority leadership before
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for floor consideration; no Republican senator cosponsored it.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever held, but all 9 cosponsors and the sponsor were Democrats and no Republican signed on, so the bill's support was entirely one-sided even though the committee chair — also a Democrat — never moved it.

industries.industry: Publicly traded corporations and their large shareholders
industries.note: The bill directly increases the cost of stock buybacks from 1% to 4%, hitting the payout method used most heavily by large companies, whose gains flow disproportionately to wealthy households and executives. Keeping the lower rate preserves the value of that payout channel.

industries.industry: Institutional investors and retirement funds holding corporate stock
industries.note: The tax can modestly reduce after-tax returns on stock held through mutual funds and pensions, but it also raises public revenue from a transaction concentrated among the largest holders.
